alternates.line: Doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: रात्रिः सैव पुनः स एव दिवसो मत्वा मुधा जन्तवो धावन्त्युद्यमिनस्तथैव निभृतप्रारब्धतत्तत्क्रियाः । व्यापारैः पुनरुक्तभूत विषयैरित्थंविधेनामुना संसारेण कदर्थिता वयमहो मोहान्न लज्जामहे ॥
verse.line: Same night, same day, the same tasks on repeat. We run in circles and call it living.
verse.translation: Thinking 'it is the same night again, the same day', creatures run about in vain, busy as ever with the tasks they have set going; with work full of the same repeated things, tormented by this round of existence, alas, out of delusion we feel no shame.
verse.why: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from a quiet place. The scene is a room at night, or perhaps the edge of a bed. He is watching the same tasks begin again. He says creatures run about in vain, busy with the same repeated things. They feel no shame out of delusion. He means time empties cities and houses, and busy people do not notice it passing. He is asking you to see the pattern underneath the work.
verse.for_you: Your work and your children fill the room, but the night comes the same way. The tasks repeat and you feel no shame. You are looking for what it is all for, and that search is the real work.
verse.try_today: Notice one task you do today that you have done before.
verse.scene_line: You are at the edge of the bed, watching the same night begin again.
asks: How do I see the pattern without blaming myself?
How do I stop running and simply see?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: नैव प्रार्थयते लाभं नालाभेनानुशोचति । धीरस्य शीतलं चित्तममृतेनैव पूरितम् ॥
verse.line: Not begging for gain, not grieving loss: a steady mind stays cool and full.
verse.translation: He does not pray for gain, nor grieve over loss. The steady one's cool mind is filled as if with nectar.
verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka about the calm of the wise. He describes someone who does not beg for gain or grieve over loss. The steady mind stays cool and full, as if with nectar, right in the middle of ordinary life.
verse.for_you: You are in the middle of the same night, the same day, the same tasks on repeat. You run in circles and call it living. The texts say calm is not found by changing places or chasing it.
verse.try_today: Notice one small task without asking what it will give you.
verse.scene_line: You are the steady one, holding the same tasks without begging for gain.
asks: How do I stop begging for gain in my own work?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha's closing advice to Rama on living in the world after the three vows.
verse.sanskrit: अन्तर्मुखः सन्सततं समस्तं कुर्वन्बहिष्ठं खलु कार्यजातम् । न खेदमायासि कदाचिदेव निराकृताहंकृतितामुपैषि ॥
verse.line: Stay anchored within while you do all your outer work, and you won't burn out.
verse.translation: Staying turned inward while doing all the outer work that comes to you, you will never grow weary, and you will be free of the sense of being the doer.
verse.why: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

prasang.title: Shiva's three vows: be a great doer, enjoyer and letter-go
prasang.summary: Vasishtha gives Rama three vows that Shiva once gave his devotee Bhringi: be a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer. A great doer acts fully and on time without clinging; a great enjoyer takes in joys and sorrows evenly, like the ocean takes in rivers; a great renouncer lets go inside. Live this way and work won't wear you out.
prasang.lesson: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha is speaking to Rama at the end of their long talk. The world still demands its daily tasks, but the mind can refuse to be dragged into them. The verse says you can keep your hands busy and your eyes open to everything around you, while your center stays turned inward, untouched by the doing. You do the work, you meet the need, you answer the call, but you do not carry the weight of it as your own burden. The outer life goes on, and the inner life rests.
verse.for_you: The same morning, the same drop-offs, the same work that asks for more. You are not failing. You are simply tired of the machine. The verse does not ask you to stop the work. It asks you to find a place inside that does not need to be fixed.
verse.try_today: Notice one small task and feel the doing in your hands without taking it into your chest.
verse.scene_line: You are at the center of a day that will not stop, and the verse asks where you are while it happens.
asks: How do I find that inward place while the work is still there?
Can I do the work and still feel like I am not the one doing it?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse.sanskrit: कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन । मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
verse.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

prasang.title: The yoga of action
prasang.summary: Krishna teaches the yoga of action: work wholeheartedly, give up clinging to outcomes, stay even in success and failure, and keep a single steady purpose.
prasang.lesson: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna on the battlefield that his right is only to the work itself, never to its fruits. He is to act with full force and care, but without letting the outcome own him or stop him. The point is to do the task completely and then let it go, keeping the mind even through success and failure.
verse.for_you: You do your work for the children and the family, but the weight of how it lands is too much to carry alone. Let the doing be enough for now. The work is yours, the rest is not.

verse.setting: Ribhu on how a free person moves through the world.
verse.sanskrit: प्राप्तकर्मकरो नित्यं शत्रुमित्रसमानदृक् । ईहितानीहितैर्मुक्तो न शोचति न काङ्क्षति ॥ सर्वस्याभिमतं वक्ता चोदितः पेशलोक्तिमान् । आशयज्ञश्च भूतानां संसारे नावसीदति ॥
verse.line: Do the work in front of you, speak gently, read people's hearts, and you won't sink in the world.
verse.translation: Always doing the work that comes, seeing friend and foe alike, free of wanting and not-wanting, such a one neither grieves nor craves. Saying what is agreeable to all, speaking gently when asked, knowing the intent of others' hearts, such a one does not sink in the world.
verse.why: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

prasang.title: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

verse.meaning: Ribhu is telling Nidagha how a person who is free inside moves through the world. The free person takes up the work that is right there. They see friend and foe with the same eye. They do not crave what they do not have, and they do not grieve for what they lost. They say what is fair, they speak gently when asked, and they read the heart of the person in front of them. Because they do all this, they do not sink in the world.
verse.for_you: You are not sinking, but the same tasks on repeat have made the water feel heavy. Ribhu's way is not to escape the work but to move through it without the weight of wanting or not wanting.
verse.try_today: Do one task at your work table with your full attention and nothing else.
verse.scene_line: You are at your work table, reading the heart of the task before you.

story.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
story.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
story.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् । अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
verse.line: Even winning everything wouldn't touch this grief that's drying me up inside.
verse.translation: I see nothing that could drive away this sorrow that is drying up my senses, not even an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom on earth or rule over the gods.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield, looking at the faces of the people he must fight. He drops his bow. He tells Krishna that even if he wins the entire world and rules the gods, nothing could ease the grief that is drying him up inside. He says he does not know what is right, cannot see which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him. The verse proposes that admitting you do not know where to turn is the exact place where clarity begins.
verse.for_you: You are in the middle of the week, looking at your own work and family, and the weight of it all has left you running on empty. You are not failing, you are simply tired of the old reasons that used to carry you.

verse.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
verse.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
verse.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
verse.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
verse.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.

verse.meaning: A teacher explains that we walk over our own hidden gold every single day and never find it. The gold is the self, the source of everything, hidden in the heart. We do not see it because we are carried away by untruth, which means we live as if the world around us is the only real thing. The teaching says we pass this treasure without knowing it, and because we do not know the spot, we never uncover it.
verse.for_you: You are walking over a hidden treasure every day, and you do not know the spot. The weight of work and the children and the family pulls you outward, so you do not feel the ground beneath your feet.
verse.try_today: Notice one ordinary thing today without trying to change it.
verse.scene_line: You are walking over hidden gold every day and never finding it.
asks: How do I find the spot when I do not even know it is there?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse.sanskrit: ऐहिकः प्राक्तनं हन्ति प्राक्तनोऽद्यतनं बलात् । सर्वदा पुरुषस्पन्दस्तत्रानुद्वेगवाञ्जयी ॥
verse.line: Today's effort and yesterday's keep wrestling. Whoever stays calm through it wins.
verse.translation: Present effort overcomes the past, and the past can overpower the present. It is always a contest of human striving, and the one who stays calm wins.
verse.why: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha sits with Rama after he has lost his kingdom and his father. Rama is drowning in grief, thinking his fate has destroyed him. Vasishtha tells him that fate is not a god or a curse. It is only yesterday's effort wearing a different mask. Today's effort can overcome it, just as a stronger ram pushes back a weaker one. The past shapes the present, but it does not own it. The one who stays calm and keeps striving wins the contest.
verse.for_you: You are tired of running, yet the race is still on. Your past effort built the life you have, but it is also the weight pulling you down. This verse does not ask you to win the whole race today. It asks you to stay calm through the wrestling.
verse.scene_line: You are standing at the edge of yesterday's effort, waiting to see if today's step will hold.
asks: How do I keep going when the past feels too heavy to lift?
Can I really change what is already built?
What does calm effort look like when I am this tired?

verse.speaker: Angiras
verse.setting: Angiras on how the wise live.
verse.sanskrit: प्रणो ह्येष यः सर्वभूतैर्विभाति विजानन् विद्वान् भवते नातिवादी । आत्मक्रीड आत्मरतिः क्रियावानेष ब्रह्मविदां वरिष्ठः ॥
verse.line: Knowing this, the wise stop arguing. Their joy is within, and they stay fully active.
verse.translation: This is the life that shines through all beings. Knowing it, the wise one does not talk over others. Delighting in the self, playing in the self, yet active, such a one is the best of the knowers of Brahman.
verse.why: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

prasang.title: Two birds on one tree
prasang.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.
prasang.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

verse.meaning: Angiras is speaking to Shaunaka about the wise. He describes a life that shines through everything. Knowing this, the wise stop arguing. Their joy is within them, and they stay fully active. This is the life that is present in all beings, and when it is known, a person no longer feels the need to compete or speak over others. They find delight in the self and play in the self, yet they remain active in the world.
verse.for_you: You are tired of the wrestling. Today's effort and yesterday's keep wrestling, and the exhaustion is real. But the joy that Angiras speaks of is not a reward for winning. It is a calm witness that sits beside you, already active in the background.
verse.try_today: Notice the calm witness beside you during a busy task.
asks: Can the calm witness feel my exhaustion?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse.sanskrit: चेतसा सर्वकर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्परः । बुद्धियोगमुपाश्रित्य मच्चित्तः सततं भव ॥
verse.line: Inwardly hand all your work to the divine, hold it as your goal, and keep your mind on it.
verse.translation: Mentally resigning all actions to me, holding me as the highest, relying on the yoga of understanding, keep your mind always on me.
verse.why: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

prasang.title: Action with devotion: surrender
prasang.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
prasang.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, where Arjuna has dropped his bow and refused to fight. The moment hangs heavy with grief and confusion. Krishna tells him to mentally resign all actions to the divine, to hold the divine as the highest goal, and to keep his mind fixed on that presence. The verse proposes that when you offer your work completely and focus your mind on what is beyond yourself, you are freed from the burden of results.
verse.for_you: The work and the children and the family still need you, and they will not wait. But the meaning you are looking for is not in a new achievement or a quieter room. It is in how you meet the day.
verse.scene_line: You stand at your kitchen counter, hands on the edge, and you offer the whole day to the one thing that holds it.
asks: How do I hand over work I do not control?
Where is the one thing I can hold in my mind today?

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: पापं चेत्पुरुषः कृत्वा कल्याणमभिपद्यते / मुच्यते सर्वपापेभ्यो महाभ्रेणेव चन्द्रमाः
verse.line: Turn to doing good after a wrong, and you come out like the moon from behind a cloud.
verse.translation: If a person who has done wrong turns to doing good, he is freed from all his wrongs, like the moon coming out from behind a great cloud.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

prasang.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.meaning: In Mithila, a wise meat-seller called a proud Brahmin ascetic to his door. The ascetic had done wrong and was searching for a way to be clean again. The meat-seller told him that if a person who has done wrong turns to doing good, he is freed from all his wrongs, like the moon coming out from behind a great cloud. The butcher said that wisdom is not hidden in caves or grand rituals. It lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly.
verse.for_you: You have looked for meaning in big ideas, but the butcher says it is in the honest work you already do and the care you give your children and parents. You do not need to do more.
verse.scene_line: You are the moon, and the cloud is just the noise you have mistaken for the sky.
asks: How do I know when I am making an enemy of my own life?
What does it mean to turn to good when I feel so empty?
Is caring for my parents the only way to find this freedom?

story.title: Bali tires of endless days and asks his father's riddle
story.story_hook: Bali had conquered everything there was to conquer, and one evening he realised he was bored.
story.summary: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day at his window he realises he is doing the same things day after day, night after night, and asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him: a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind; win it over, by practice, and everything is won.
story.lesson: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

anchor.speaker: Virochana
anchor.setting: Bali's father Virochana tells him the secret of mastering the mind.
anchor.sanskrit: एषा ह्यत्यन्तदुष्प्रापा सुप्रापा च महामते । अनभ्यस्तातिदुष्प्रापा स्वभ्यस्ता प्राप्यते सुखम् ॥
anchor.line: Unpractised, it feels impossible. Well practised, it comes easily.
anchor.translation: This is extremely hard to attain and also easy, great-minded one: unpractised, it is very hard to reach; well practised, it comes easily.
anchor.why: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

story.for_you: You have done the conquering, the building, the showing up. Now you stand at the window and feel the loop. The children, the work, the family, they are not the problem. The mind is running the machine, and it is tired.

queries.hook: The wish to understand what these texts teach, and to find in them something steady to lean on.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: What passes cannot fill the heart; turning toward what lasts gives each day a quiet purpose.
queries.act: Turn toward what lasts: serve, study, reflect daily, and offer your work to something beyond yourself.
queries.story: A story of a student who came to a teacher with questions and was led, step by step, toward the truth.

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: One of the best-known verses of the Upanishad, on the God within all.
verse.sanskrit: एको देवः सर्वभूतेषु गूढः सर्वव्यापी सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा। कर्माध्यक्षः सर्वभूताधिवासः साक्षी चेता केवलो निर्गुणश्च ॥
verse.line: One God is hidden in every being: the inner self of all, the quiet witness of all we do.
verse.translation: One God is hidden in all beings: all-pervading, the inner self of every being, overseer of all action, dwelling in all beings, the witness, pure awareness, alone, beyond all qualities.
verse.why: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

prasang.title: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

verse.meaning: The Seer speaks to the Seekers. They have been asking what governs the world, what causes joy and sorrow. The Seer tells them that the answer is not far away. One God is hidden in every being. This is the inner self of all, the quiet witness of everything we do, pure awareness that lives in every heart, alone and beyond all qualities. The point is that true refuge is found only after you have honestly asked the hard questions.
verse.for_you: You have been running on empty and asking what it is all for. The text says that the answer is not outside you. The one who watches the exhaustion, the children, the work, is the quiet witness already living inside you.
verse.try_today: Notice the one who is watching the exhaustion and the search.
verse.scene_line: You are the quiet witness of your own life, waiting to be seen.

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: On the joy at the heart of things.
verse.sanskrit: यद्वै तत् सुकृतम् रसो वै सः रसꣳह्येवायं लब्ध्वाऽऽनन्दी भवति ।
verse.line: It is the very flavour of life. Whoever tastes it is filled with joy.
verse.translation: That which is well made is the essence itself. Having found that essence, a person becomes joyful.
verse.why: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

prasang.title: The measure of joy
prasang.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.
prasang.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

verse.meaning: The teacher asks the students what the very essence of life is. He does not point to wealth or power. He says that the well-made essence itself is the source of joy. A person who finds this essence becomes truly joyful.
verse.for_you: You are looking for something deeper, and this is the pattern underneath it. The joy you are missing is not something you buy or achieve. It is the very flavour of life, waiting to be tasted. You are already filled with it.
verse.try_today: Notice one small moment of flavour in your day, without trying to change it.
verse.scene_line: You are standing before the teacher, waiting to hear the measure of true joy.
asks: How do I taste this essence when I am so busy?
What does it mean to be well-made in my life right now?
How does this joy free me from the fear of not being enough?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: स्वाराज्ये भैक्षवृत्तौ च लाभालाभे जने वने । निर्विकल्पस्वभावस्य न विशेषोऽस्ति योगिनः ॥
verse.line: Throne or begging bowl, gain or loss, crowd or solitude: a steady person stays the same.
verse.translation: For the yogi of steady nature there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, gain and loss, the crowd and the forest.

words.en: of the one with undoubting nature

verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka, who has renounced his throne and sits in a forest. He tells him that the yogi of steady nature feels no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms. For this person, there is no contrast between gain and loss, between the crowd and the forest. The verse says that calm is not found by running away or changing places. It is found in how you hold the ordinary life that is already here.
verse.for_you: You have left the demands of work and the noise of the house to sit in the quiet of your own mind, yet the search for meaning still moves like a restless wind. The verse shows that peace is not a new place you reach.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own quiet room, holding the kingdom of your day and the bowl of your breath as one.
asks: What is the one thing I can hold steady today?
How does my search for meaning change if I stop moving?
Can I find the same peace in the kitchen and in the silence?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
verse.sanskrit: श्रद्धस्व तात श्रद्धस्व नात्र मोऽहं कुरुष्व भोः । ज्ञानस्वरूपो भगवानात्मा त्वं प्रकृतेः परः ॥
verse.line: Have faith, my child, have faith. You are more than everything that happens to you.
verse.translation: Have faith, my son, have faith. Do not be confused about this. You are knowledge itself, the Lord, the Self beyond nature.
verse.why: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

prasang.title: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka, who has already begun to see the truth. He presses the point further. You are not the doer, not the body, not the mind with its endless likes and dislikes. You are the awareness in which all of this happens. The thoughts, the roles, the weight of the kingdom, the ache of the body, they are all like waves on a deep ocean. You are the ocean. Let the waves rise and fall without losing yourself. Have faith in what you are beyond every role and every outcome.
verse.for_you: The roles are heavy right now. The work, the children, the family. But you are not the roles. You are the space in which they happen. You are the quiet witness. The exhaustion is real, but it is a wave. You are the ocean.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today where you are the witness, not the role.
verse.scene_line: You are the ocean, Janaka, and the kingdom is a wave.
asks: How do I stop being the roles I play?
Can I rest in the witness without feeling lazy?

verse.speaker: Rama
verse.setting: Rama, ending his questions, asks for one practical skill.
verse.sanskrit: व्यवहारवतो युक्त्या दुःखं नायाति मे यया । अथवा व्यवहारस्य ब्रूत तां युक्तिमुत्तमाम् ॥
verse.line: Teach me how to keep working in the world without the work filling me with sorrow.
verse.translation: Tell me the skill by which sorrow doesn't come to me while I go about my work, or else tell me the best way of dealing with life itself.
verse.why: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

prasang.title: Rama asks how to live in the world without being crushed by it
prasang.summary: After his lament Rama turns to questions. How did King Janaka and others stay free while running kingdoms? How can a person work in the world untouched, like water on a lotus leaf? He asks for one practical skill that lets him work without sorrow.
prasang.story_hook: Having said what was wrong, Rama finally asked the question that matters: how do the wise do it?
prasang.lesson: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

verse.meaning: Rama asks how to keep working in the world without the work filling me with sorrow. He has just finished asking about the nature of existence and the pain of living. Now he wants a practical skill. The answer is not to escape the world, but to change how you meet it. The skill is to rest in the self that watches everything happen. When you do that, your actions continue but they no longer own you. The work is done, but the sorrow does not arrive.
verse.for_you: You are looking for a deeper place to stand while the work is still there. The skill is not to do less, but to feel less owned by what you do. The children and the tasks are still yours, but they are not the whole of you.
verse.try_today: When you finish one task, pause and notice the watcher.
verse.scene_line: You are Rama, asking how to serve without being crushed.
asks: How do I find the watcher when the work is loud?
Can the watcher feel tired like the rest of me?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna describes those whom he lifts out of the sea of mortality (12.7).
verse.sanskrit: ये तु सर्वाणि कर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्पराः । अनन्येनैव योगेन मां ध्यायन्त उपासते ॥ तेषामहं समुद्धर्ता मृत्युसंसारसागरात् । भवामि नचिरात्पार्थ मय्यावेशितचेतसाम् ॥
verse.line: Lay your work in me and keep your mind on me; I soon lift you out of the drowning sea.
verse.translation: But those who lay all their actions in me, intent on me, and worship me meditating with single-minded yoga — for them, whose minds are set on me, I soon become the one who lifts them out of the ocean of death and rebirth, Partha.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just finished describing those who are dear to him and now turns to the ones who are in danger of drowning. He says that those who give up the results of their actions and fix their minds on him, worshiping with single-minded focus, will be lifted out of the ocean of birth and death. He is offering a way to keep working without being swallowed by the work.
verse.for_you: You are in the middle of your week, and the question from yesterday still sits in your chest. The work itself is not the enemy, but the way it fills you with sorrow is. You have laid your actions at the edge of the day.
verse.try_today: At the end of the workday, before you turn to anything else, set the day down.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the edge of the day, offering the work back to the one who asked for it.
asks: How do I let the work go without feeling lazy?

What does it mean to fix my mind on something I cannot see?

story.title: Bhrigu learns from his father
story.story_hook: Bhrigu asked his father the biggest question there is, and got only a hint in reply.
story.summary: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him what is ultimate. Varuna gives only a clue and tells him to reflect. Bhrigu comes back four times with answers (food, breath, mind, understanding) and each time is sent back to go deeper, until he discovers that everything is born from joy, lives by joy and returns to joy.
story.lesson: A wise parent lets a child discover the answer instead of handing it over.

anchor.speaker: Narrator
anchor.setting: Bhrigu's final discovery after four returns to his father.
anchor.sanskrit: आनन्दो ब्रह्मेति व्यजानात्। आनन्दाध्येव खल्विमानि भूतानि जायन्ते । आनन्देन जातानि जीवन्ति । आनन्दं प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्तीति । सैषा भार्गवी वारुणी विद्या । परमे व्योमन्प्रतिष्ठिता ।स य एवं वेद प्रतितिष्ठति ।
anchor.line: At last Bhrigu saw: from joy all beings are born, by joy they live, into joy they return.
anchor.translation: He understood that joy is Brahman. From joy these beings are born, by joy they live once born, and into joy they enter at death. This is the wisdom of Bhrigu and Varuna, established in the highest space. Whoever knows this becomes established.
